reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A direct communication between the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk in the presence of two separate, normally formed semilunar valves
This distinguishes it from truncus arteriosus, which has a single common valve and trunk
A large window produces a substantial left-to-right shunt with pulmonary overcirculation and early heart failure
Physiology resembles a large patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect, with a wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses
Because the shunt is typically large, pulmonary vascular obstructive disease can develop early if repair is delayed
Associated anomalies include interrupted aortic arch and anomalous coronary origin, which affect surgical planning
Early surgical closure, usually with a patch, restores normal separation of the circulations
reference.pathophysiology: An aortopulmonary window results from incomplete septation of the embryonic truncus arteriosus, leaving a defect in the wall shared by the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk while two distinct semilunar valves still form. The communication permits a large left-to-right shunt from the high-pressure aorta into the pulmonary circulation. As pulmonary vascular resistance falls after birth, pulmonary blood flow increases markedly, imposing volume loading on the left heart and causing congestive failure. The persistently elevated pulmonary flow and pressure can drive early and potentially irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive disease. The lesion may be isolated or associated with other anomalies such as interrupted aortic arch, and coronary artery origins can be involved near the defect.
additionalDifferentials: Coronary artery fistula draining to the pulmonary artery
Pulmonary atresia with major aortopulmonary collaterals
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to demonstrate the defect and confirm two separate semilunar valves
Cardiac CT or MR angiography to define the window and associated arch or coronary anomalies
Cardiac catheterisation to quantify the shunt and assess pulmonary vascular resistance
Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora
Assessment for interrupted aortic arch and anomalous coronary origins
redFlags: Early heart failure from a large left-to-right shunt
Signs of rapidly progressive pulmonary vascular obstructive disease
Coexisting interrupted aortic arch or duct-dependent circulation
Anomalous coronary origin near the defect complicating repair
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent after early surgical closure before pulmonary vascular disease develops, whereas delayed repair risks irreversible pulmonary hypertension and a poor long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Confusing the lesion with truncus arteriosus by not confirming two separate semilunar valves
Mistaking it for a large patent ductus and missing the aortopulmonary communication
Delaying repair and allowing fixed pulmonary vascular disease to develop
Overlooking associated interrupted aortic arch or coronary anomalies
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Close the defect surgically early, typically by patch closure on cardiopulmonary bypass in infancy, before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops
Stabilise preoperative heart failure from pulmonary over-circulation with diuretics, afterload reduction and nutritional support
Repair associated anomalies such as interrupted aortic arch and anomalous coronary origin at the same operation, guided by preoperative imaging
Assess pulmonary vascular resistance by catheterisation in late-presenting cases and manage established pulmonary hypertension with targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy
Provide postoperative surveillance for residual shunt, pulmonary hypertension and arrhythmia, with endocarditis-prevention measures
Coordinate care through a congenital cardiology and cardiac surgery multidisciplinary team
